d.title: Which of them is actually a metric, and why you should care
d.caption: **The triangle inequality is the condition with consequences**, because it is what lets a ball tree or KD-tree discard a whole branch: if the query is far from a region's centre, everything inside is far too. Break it and the pruning is unsound. **Squared Euclidean breaks it and is used everywhere anyway**, because it ranks identically to Euclidean and skips a square root — safe wherever only the order matters, unsafe the moment the number is averaged or thresholded.

state: not one - but it is k-means inertia
a metric - the sqrt of the divergence

d.title: 7, 5, 4.4979, 4 - the whole story of p
d.caption: **One formula, and p decides how much a single large difference dominates.** The difference vector is (3, 4, 0): at p = 1 both count their full size and add to 7; as p rises the 4 takes over; at the limit Chebyshev returns 4 and has discarded the 3 entirely. **The unit ball is the picture to carry** — a diamond at L1, a circle at L2, a square at L∞ — and the diamond having its corners on the axes is exactly why L1 regularisation produces exact zeros where L2 does not.

state: the same order as L2, no sqrt

d.title: No vector index offers cosine, and none needs to
d.caption: **On L2-normalised vectors, squared Euclidean equals 2 − 2·cos** — a decreasing function of cosine, so L2 search, inner-product search and cosine search return the same ranking. Normalise once at indexing time and the index's metric stops being a modelling decision. **The failure is forgetting one side:** normalise at indexing and not at query time and the scores are wrong in a way that still looks plausible — the ranking distorts rather than breaking, so nothing errors and recall quietly drops.

nodes.label: Nothing errors; recall drops
nodes.sub: which is why it survives review

d.title: Euclidean says 2.83 twice; Mahalanobis says 2.04 and 9.04
d.caption: **The features correlate at 0.9, so one being high while the other is low almost never happens** — and Euclidean cannot express that, because it has no idea the features are related. A factor of four and a half between two points it calls equidistant is why Mahalanobis is the standard multivariate outlier tool: a record whose every individual field is unremarkable can still be an impossible combination. **And it is just Euclidean distance after whitening**, which is both the one-sentence explanation and a cheaper implementation route.

state: ordinary - the data goes this way
shrink it, or reduce the dimension

d.title: The shift Jensen-Shannon cannot see
d.caption: **Wasserstein returned 1, 5 and 50 for shifts of 1, 5 and 50. Jensen-Shannon returned 0.8326 for all three.** Once the supports are disjoint, every divergence built on pointwise probability ratios is saturated — it can say the distributions do not overlap and nothing about how far apart they are, so a sensor drifting by one unit and by fifty are the same number. **KL has the same blind spot and two more besides:** it is asymmetric, 0.3195 one way and 0.3713 the other, and it is infinite the moment the second distribution has a zero where the first does not.

d.title: One pair of counts, three metrics, three verdicts
d.caption: **The 0-against-1 coordinate is the entire disagreement.** Euclidean sees a difference of 1 among numbers like 10 and 12, and shrugs. Canberra divides each difference by the sum of that pair, so 0 → 1 is a *complete* change contributing a full 1.0 — which is why it dominates at 1.09. Bray-Curtis normalises by the grand total instead, so the same coordinate barely moves it. **Pick by whether a change from zero is meaningful or is noise**, because Canberra will amplify exactly whichever it is.

state: the 10->12 term; the zero barely registers

d.title: The farthest point goes from 53x to 12% farther
d.caption: **That is why every vector database is more complicated than a linear scan.** The nearest neighbour still exists in a thousand dimensions, but it is barely distinguishable from the farthest, so a little noise reorders the results and a pruning bound excludes almost nothing — exact tree search degenerates to a scan. **Approximate indexes are forced by this table, not chosen.** Note also where the contrast crosses 1.0: somewhere between 10 and 100 dimensions, far below any real embedding.

d.title: Agreeing on a birth date is worth eleven bits; on gender, one
d.caption: **It is all in `u`.** Two random people almost never share a date of birth, so `u` is 0.0005 and agreement is worth +10.89 bits; they agree on gender half the time, so `u` is 0.5 and agreement is worth +0.97. **Now read the gender row across:** +0.97 for agreement and −4.64 for disagreement, because matching pairs disagree only 2% of the time. A reliably recorded low-cardinality field is nearly useless for confirming a match and excellent for ruling one out — and one hand-tuned weight per field cannot say that.

d.title: The two patterns most hand-built scorers rank backwards
d.caption: **A changed surname confirmed by birth date and postcode scores +15.49. Both names matching with no birth date scores +6.23.** Names feel more identifying than they are: two different people sharing a common name is an ordinary occurrence, while two random people sharing a date of birth and a postcode is not. The first case is a woman who married; the second is a coincidence a scorer should hesitate over — which is exactly where the middle band in section 05 is for.

d.title: Five billion pairs, cut to 0.039% of the work
d.caption: **A hundred thousand records is five billion pairs, and a hundred thousand is a small dataset** — so blocking is not an optimisation, it is what makes record linkage possible. **But every row buys that reduction with recall:** a true match whose records disagree on the blocking key is never generated as a candidate, and no amount of downstream scoring recovers it. Those are also the dirtiest records, which is why production pipelines run several passes on different keys and union the candidates rather than choosing the best key.

d.title: Three regions, because for some scores the evidence genuinely does not settle it
d.caption: **Collapsing to a single threshold does not remove the uncertain pairs — it only stops you knowing which they were**, since each is silently assigned to whichever side of the line it fell on. **And which error to prefer is a property of the application, not the model:** merging two patients' records is a clinical safety incident, so healthcare linkage sets a high upper threshold and staffs a large queue; a duplicate mailing is an annoyance, so marketing deduplication reverses the trade. Decide that before tuning anything.

nodes.label: Above the upper threshold: link
nodes.sub: risk: two people merged into one

nodes.label: Between: send to a human
nodes.sub: size this band to your review capacity

nodes.label: Below the lower: do not link
Which risk is worse is the application's

d.title: What the merged record says, and how to defend it later
d.caption: **This is the half that reaches the user**, and a pipeline with excellent precision and no survivorship policy produces a record whose address is whichever row was processed first. **The branch most often got wrong is the last one:** a date of birth should not change, so two different ones on records you merged is evidence the match was wrong rather than a field to pick a winner for. And keep per-field lineage with the constituent records — a destructive merge turns a recoverable linkage error into permanent data loss.
